newsitem.title: BELGIUM: European Peoples Party consolidates power.
newsitem.headline: European Peoples Party consolidates power.

text.p: The European Union's Christian Democrats are to join up with sister parties in Central and Eastern Europe in a move to make their European Peoples Party the main political force in an enlarged EU.

The EPP, which has 20 member parties in the EU and is the second largest political group in the European Parliament, believes that by opening its arms to Christian Democrat parties in the nine states seeking EU membership, it can boost their chances of winning elections and shaping Europe's future.
"We will help them as much as possible to enlarge their electoral base," Dutch Christian Democrat MEP Wim van Velzen told Reuters on Thursday. "It is good for them and good for us."
Through its new members to the east, the EPP hoped to contribute to the debate about EU enlargement, Van Velzen added.
The Dutch MEP is the chairman of the EPP's parent body, the European Union of Christian Democrats (EUCD), and will over the next two years preside over its effective demise.
Founded 70 years ago, the loosely-structured EUCD now groups 46 parties from western and eastern Europe.

But the EPP has become increasingly concerned by the EPP-EUCD overlap and the EUCD's unwieldy decision-making procedure, and increasingly convinced of the need to concentrate on parties which could be in the European Parliament in the foreseeable future.
"These people will be negotiating for EU accession. It makes sense to have them in a simple, transparent structure. The EUCD is huge and nothing actually happens," one EPP official said.

After much debate, the EUCD adopted a declaration on October 6 agreeing to the reform and stating: "Our objective must be to make the EPP the principal political force of the European Parliament and of the EU".

On October 17, the EPP's political bureau will consider offering observer and later associate membership to seven parties in Eastern and Central Europe. A further 13 could be admitted before December 1998.
The Party of European Socialists, which holds most seats in the European Parliament, decided in February 1995 to offer observer status to its sister parties in the former Soviet Bloc.

Among its senior members, the EPP can boast of five EU prime ministers, three leaders of parties in coalition governments, European Commission President Jacques Santer and Farm Commissioner Franz Fischler.
Van Velzen said he was optimistic forthcoming elections would put Christian Democrats in government in Romania, Bulgaria, Lithuania and Estonia, with the help of the EPP.
"We want to establish sane, moderate democratic parties who will have to do some unpopular things. They will not do well in elections without help, including economic help," the official added.
As well as swelling its wider European ranks, the EPP hopes further reforms will soon increase the number of seats it holds in the European Parliament.
Portugal's Social Democrat Party (PSD) is due to decided on November 16 whether its six MEPs should defect to the EPP from the small Liberal group in the European Parliament.

"It is difficult for the PSD to have a voice in Europe if it is not in a big European party," MEP Antonio Capucho, the leader of the PSD team and an EP vice-president, told Reuters, adding that the PSD did not have much ideological affinity with the Liberals.
In addition, issues of concern to southern European tended to be left aside in the Liberal group, which is largely composed of Belgians, Danes, Finn and Dutch, he said. REUTER
